\subsection{Attribution, value function and conclusions}
\label{sec:setting}
A trained model $f$ maps an instance $x$ with $d$ raw attributes to a score. Each raw attribute is one player; a categorical attribute is one player and is one-hot encoded inside the model wrapper.
The value function of a coalition $S$ is the marginal (interventional) expectation of the score when the attributes outside $S$ are drawn from a background of $B=50$ training rows, drawn once per dataset and seed and held fixed in every experiment of this paper.
The background is thus part of the definition of the attribution, and the Shapley value $\phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^d$ of this value function is the exact reference.

\paragraph{Shapley attribution and its estimators.}
SHAP casts feature attribution as the Shapley value of a value function that removes features \citep{lundberg2017}; the value function may be marginal or conditional \citep{chen2020,sundararajan2020,kumar2020}, and removal-based explanations share this structure \citep{covert2020removal}.
Model-agnostic estimation is randomised: Kernel SHAP and its unbiased variant with variance and convergence estimates \citep{covert2021}, permutation and antithetic sampling \citep{mitchell2022}, Leverage SHAP with guarantees \citep{musco2025}, regression-adjusted Monte Carlo \citep{witter2025regadj} and SHAP-IQ \citep{fumagalli2023}; \citet{chen2023algorithms} survey the algorithms.
Tree ensembles admit a deterministic algorithm \citep{lundberg2020trees}.
These works report the error to the exact Shapley value, usually in $\ell_2$ and averaged over instances, at chosen budgets.
They do not ask whether one run at a deployment budget supports the conclusion a reader draws from it for a given instance, nor whether the run can detect its own failure.

\paragraph{Top-$k$ identification.}
Whether an estimated ordering yields the right top-$k$ is asked from the estimator side: Shapley bandits for top-$k$ identification \citep{kolpaczki2021bandits} and antithetic sampling for top-$k$ Shapley identification \citep{kolpaczki2025antithetic} design algorithms with sampling guarantees.
We instead measure deployed default estimators on trained tabular models and map the conditions under which one run identifies the right features.
\citet{covert2021} already give within-run variance and convergence detection, so what we add to the single-run check is its validation against the top-$k$ conclusion.
\citet{huang2023} question what Shapley values say about a model; we only bound scope by holding the value function fixed.

\paragraph{Disagreement and robustness.}
\citet{krishna2022} and \citet{neely2021} study disagreement between explanation methods; \citet{alvarez2018} and \citet{ghorbani2019fragile} study sensitivity to input perturbation; \citet{visani2022lime} study LIME stability under resampling; \citet{yuan2022} study background size for deep models.
We fix the model, the value function and the instance, and isolate the explainer's own randomness against an exact reference, then compare it with background and retraining noise.

\paragraph{Multiplicity as a yardstick.}
Predictive multiplicity and the Rashomon set \citep{marx2020,fisher2019,dong2020cloud} give the variability between equally accurate models; ShapleyVIC \citep{shapleyvic2022} applies this to Shapley importance.
We use it as a noise floor for explainer noise, not as the target.

\paragraph{Metrics and data.}
We measure the stability of selected sets with the index of \citet{nogueira2018} and the agreement of rankings with rank-biased overlap \citep{webber2010}.
The data are German Credit, the ACS tasks of \citet{ding2021}, and other public tabular sets (Section~\ref{sec:design}); tabular deep models follow \citet{gorishniy2021}.

cd /hutian/repo/paper; cat > intro.tex <<'E'
Feature attributions are computed once and read once.
For a tabular model, a SHAP value per feature is estimated by a randomised, budget-limited algorithm, and the reader then draws a conclusion from the single result: which feature mattered most, which three mattered, whether a feature pushed the score up or down.
The literature on Shapley estimators measures how close an estimate is to the exact Shapley value, usually in $\ell_2$, averaged over instances and at chosen budgets \citep{lundberg2017,covert2021,mitchell2022,musco2025}.
A small average error does not say that a particular run returns the conclusion the exact values would give: when two features are nearly tied, a tiny error swaps them.
Our question is therefore how far one randomised, budget-limited SHAP run can be treated as a reliable basis for a prediction, where the prediction is the conclusion a reader draws.

We answer it for the unchanged \texttt{shap} Kernel explainer and two sampled alternatives, on four model classes and five public tabular datasets, with the value function fixed so that the randomness of the explainer is not confused with the choice of what is explained (Section~\ref{sec:setting}).
The reference is the exact Shapley value of that value function, obtained by enumerating all coalitions once per instance, so every run is scored against the quantity it estimates.
For each instance we measure the probability $P_c$ that a run returns the exact top-$k$ set, a tolerance-aware version that forgives swaps across an exact near tie, and the agreement of two runs, and we summarise a dataset--model cell by the share of its instances for which one run is correct with probability at least $0.9$.
We compare the explainer's own noise with the noise from drawing another background and from retraining the model, and we test whether a certificate computed from one run is a better check than running twice.

\paragraph{Results.}
In these cells the answer is conditional, and the condition is explicit.
(i)~At the \texttt{shap} default budget, one run returns the exact top-3 set with probability at least $0.9$ for $0.90$--$1.00$ of the instances of each cell on the two datasets with $d\ge16$, and for every instance once swaps across near ties are forgiven; at half of all coalitions on the three smaller datasets the strict share is $0.79$--$1.00$ (Section~\ref{sec:headline}).
(ii)~The failures are the instances whose third and fourth features are nearly tied; the mean correlation with the exact values is above $0.98$ at every budget of at least three times the number of features and would not have warned of them (Section~\ref{sec:margin}).
(iii)~Below about $3d$ coalitions, with a feature-selecting setting such as \texttt{num\_features(10)}, or on the instances with the smallest margins, a run cannot be treated as reliable; the budget that a margin requires does not follow the $1/g^2$ law that a Gaussian argument suggests (Section~\ref{sec:budget}).
(iv)~Two runs of the explainer agree on the top-3 set far more often ($0.91$--$0.99$ at the reference budget) than two backgrounds ($0.27$--$0.69$) or two retrained models ($0.14$--$0.73$): for the conclusions we study, one run is not the weakest link (Section~\ref{sec:floors}).
(v)~A certificate from one run is not a clear improvement over running twice (Section~\ref{sec:cert}); this is a negative result of the study.

\paragraph{Scope.}
We study the explainer's randomness for a fixed value function and a fixed background, on tables with at most $20$ attributes, so that the exact reference exists; five datasets are five observations of the setting, so the findings are per dataset and carry no dataset-level interval.
All code, the result tables behind every figure and table, and the reproduction notes are provided with the paper.
E

\paragraph{Data and models.}
We use five public binary-classification tables, chosen to span the number of players $d$: German Credit ($d=20$, 1000 rows), ACS Employment ($d=16$) and ACS Income ($d=10$) from the 2018 one-year person file for California \citep{ding2021}, Pima Indians Diabetes ($d=8$) and Give Me Some Credit ($d=10$).
For each dataset we fit logistic regression (LR), a random forest (RF, 100 trees, minimum leaf size 5), gradient boosting (XGBoost, 200 trees, depth 4) and a scikit-learn MLP, on one train/test split; training sets are capped at 30\,000 rows.
Held-out AUC and the output space explained are in Table~\ref{tab:design} (Appendix~\ref{app:tables}).
The instances to explain are drawn at random from the test split, not selected by margin: 40 for German Credit, 60 for ACS Employment and 100 for each of the other datasets.
The unit of generalisation is the dataset: with five populations we report each dataset on its own, and any pooled statement is descriptive.

\paragraph{Estimators and budgets.}
We run (i) the unchanged \texttt{KernelExplainer} of the \texttt{shap} package (version 0.51.0) with its default sampling, with \texttt{l1\_reg} set to \texttt{False}, \texttt{"auto"} (the default) and \texttt{"num\_features(10)"}; (ii) unbiased paired Kernel SHAP \citep{covert2021}; and (iii) antithetic permutation sampling \citep{mitchell2022}.
The \texttt{shap} default budget is $m=2d+2048$ coalitions; for $d\le10$ this exceeds the $2^d-2$ non-trivial coalitions, so the default enumerates all of them and is deterministic.
For $d\ge16$ we use $m\in\{32,64,128,256,1024,2d{+}2048,4096,16384\}$; for $d\le10$ we use $5$, $10$, $15$, $25$ and $50\%$ of the $2^d-2$ coalitions plus the default.
Each run costs $(m+1)B+1$ model evaluations (background included), and comparisons between estimators are made at equal evaluations; the antithetic estimator uses whole pairs of permutations and never exceeds $m$.
Each cell is repeated $R=100$ times with independent seeds, except for German LR ($R=30$), German and ACS-Employment MLP ($R=60$) and ACS-Employment LR ($R=30$), which were cut for cost; the deterministic default budgets at $d\le10$ have $R=1$.

The first full draft of the paper is on `dev`, and the main text is about 8.6 of the 9 pages. It is not ready to offer as a version yet. The checklist's compute answer is still a `TODO` placeholder, and a few result cells are not final. The paper builds locally at 19 pages in all, with the references starting on page 9.

- **What's written:** The abstract, introduction, results, discussion and limitations, an appendix of tables, and the NeurIPS checklist. Every number comes from the delivered result tables and figure data.
- **What the results say:** At the shap default budget, one run returns the exact top-3 set for 0.90–1.00 of instances on the two larger datasets, and for all instances once swaps across near ties are forgiven. Failures sit in the smallest-margin instances. Two runs of the explainer agree far more often (0.91–0.99) than two backgrounds (0.27–0.69) or two retrained models (0.14–0.73). A one-run certificate is not a clear win over running twice. The 1/g² budget law is not supported on this grid.
- **What I changed:**
  - I removed a related-work paragraph that claimed metrics the study never computed.
  - I left Figure 1 out of the main text, since it shows no failure.
  - I reworded my own draft sentences that the tables contradicted.
- **Still open:**
  - German GBM has 37 of 40 instances.
  - RF and GBM at d ≥ 16 lack the smallest budgets.
  - Floors for the German and ACS-Employment MLPs are missing.
  - The background-sensitivity tables are not delivered.
  - Total CPU-hours and failed runs for the checklist are not yet available.
- **Asked of analysis (`experiment-repo`#7):** to check what each number is said to be, and to send the CPU-hours total. I also asked why shap Kernel on LR shows variance at the two smallest Pima budgets.

I'll rewrite only the sentences that carry the pending numbers once they are final. Then I'll fill the checklist and offer a version.
